words.exampleEn: Hangul is fun.
words.usageNote: The name of the Korean writing system you just learned.
words.soundNote: 한글은 links as hangeureun (the ㄹ moves into 은), and 있어요 is heard as isseoyo, not it-eoyo.

words.exampleEn: I study Korean.
words.usageNote: 한국 (Korea) + 어 (language).

words.exampleEn: The speech is fast.
words.usageNote: Spoken language in general. Also appears in 말하다 (to speak).

words.exampleEn: This word is easy.
words.usageNote: What you are learning right now: individual words.

words.exampleEn: I listen to the sound.
words.usageNote: Any sound — a voice, music, or noise.

words.exampleEn: I read a book.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 읽어요.
words.formNote: 읽다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 읽어요 by adding -어요: the ㄹ of the ㄺ batchim stays put and the ㄱ moves to start the next syllable, so it sounds like il-geo-yo.
words.soundNote: 책을 links lightly in speech: 책을 → 채글, so the example sounds closer to chae-geul il-geo-yo.

words.exampleEn: I listen to music.
words.usageNote: Irregular: ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel, so the polite form is 들어요.
words.formNote: 듣다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 들어요 because ㄷ irregular verbs change ㄷ to ㄹ before a vowel ending: 듣 + 어요 → 들어요.
words.soundNote: 음악을 links in speech: 음악을 → 으마글, so the example sounds closer to eu-ma-geul deu-reo-yo.

words.exampleEn: I write my name.
words.usageNote: Also means "to use" and "to wear (a hat/glasses)". Polite form: 써요.
words.formNote: 쓰다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 써요 because the ㅡ vowel drops before -어요.

words.exampleEn: I read a sentence.
words.usageNote: Words become sentences — the next step after this section.

words.exampleEn: Practice is needed.
words.usageNote: 연습하다 = to practice.
words.soundNote: 연습이 links as yeonseubi, and 필요 is heard as piryo, not pil-yo — the ㄹ moves into 요.

words.exampleEn: Hello. I am a student.
words.usageNote: Safe polite greeting for most situations, any time of day.

words.exampleEn: Thank you very much.
words.usageNote: Formal-polite thank you. Works everywhere.

words.exampleEn: Yes, that's right.
words.usageNote: Also used as "I see / uh-huh" while listening.
words.soundNote: 맞아요 is heard as majayo, not mat-ayo — the ㅈ batchim links into the next syllable.

words.exampleEn: No, it's okay.
words.usageNote: Polite no. Casual form: 아니.

words.exampleEn: Water, please.
words.usageNote: Put the thing you want before it: [thing] + 주세요.

words.exampleEn: Sorry for being late.
words.usageNote: Formal-polite apology, safe with strangers.
words.soundNote: 늦어서 is heard as neujeoseo, not neut-eo-seo — the ㅈ batchim links into the next syllable.

words.exampleEn: It's okay. Don't worry.
words.usageNote: Also "no thanks" when offered something.

words.exampleEn: Please help me.
words.usageNote: 돕다 (to help) + 주세요 (please do for me).

words.exampleEn: One moment. I'll be right back.
words.usageNote: Also used to pass through a crowd, like "excuse me".

words.exampleEn: I don't really know.
words.usageNote: From 모르다 (to not know).

words.exampleEn: Yes, got it.
words.usageNote: From 알다 (to know). More formal: 알겠습니다.

words.exampleEn: I am a student.
words.usageNote: Humble/polite "I". Use with people you don't know well.

words.exampleEn: I like coffee. (casual)
words.usageNote: Casual "I" — only with close friends or younger people.
words.soundNote: 좋아해 is heard as joahae — the ㅎ of 좋 drops before the vowel.

words.exampleEn: Where are you going? (casual)
words.usageNote: Casual only. Koreans often use a name or title instead of "you".

words.exampleEn: We are friends.
words.usageNote: Also "our": 우리 집 (our house), even when it's just yours.

words.exampleEn: Who is that person?
words.usageNote: 한국 사람 = a Korean person.

words.exampleEn: I meet a friend.
words.usageNote: Usually implies same age in Korean culture.

words.exampleEn: My friend is a student.
Thank you, teacher.
words.usageNote: 님 is an honorific ending. Also a polite way to address strangers.

words.exampleEn: What is your name?
Who is it?
words.usageNote: As the subject it becomes 누가: 누가 왔어요? (Who came?)

words.exampleEn: This book, please.
words.usageNote: Goes before a noun: 이 사람 (this person). Near the speaker.

words.exampleEn: I know that person.
words.usageNote: Near the listener, or something already mentioned.

words.exampleEn: That house over there is big.
words.usageNote: Far from both speaker and listener. Same spelling as 저 (I) — context decides.
words.soundNote: 집이 is heard as jibi, not jip-i — the ㅂ batchim links into the next syllable.

words.exampleEn: What is this?
words.usageNote: Spoken form of 이것. Extremely common when pointing.

words.exampleEn: Please give me that.
words.usageNote: Spoken form of 그것.

words.exampleEn: How much is that one over there?
words.usageNote: Spoken form of 저것.

words.exampleEn: This is mine.
words.usageNote: A grammar workhorse: 제 것 = my thing = mine. Often shortened to 거.
words.soundNote: 것은 and 것이에요 both link the ㅅ batchim forward: i-geo-seun, geo-si-e-yo.

words.exampleEn: What are you eating?
words.usageNote: Spoken form of 무엇.

words.exampleEn: This book is fun.
words.soundNote: 책은 is heard as chaegeun — the ㄱ batchim links forward into 은.

words.exampleEn: Please call me.
words.usageNote: 전화하다 = to make a phone call.

words.exampleEn: Please sit here.
It's there.
words.usageNote: Near the listener, or a place already mentioned.
words.soundNote: 있어요 is heard as isseoyo, not it-eoyo.

words.exampleEn: The bathroom is over there.
words.usageNote: Also used to get attention: 저기요! (Excuse me!)

words.exampleEn: I'm going home.
words.soundNote: 집에 is heard as jibe, not jip-e — the ㅂ batchim links into 에.

words.exampleEn: I go to school.
I work at a company.
Where is the bathroom?
words.usageNote: A survival essential.

words.exampleEn: The station is close.
words.usageNote: 서울역 = Seoul Station.

words.exampleEn: I'm going now.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 가요. 가다 also describes time passing — see its own sense card.
words.formNote: 가다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 가요 because polite present uses the stem 가 plus -요.

words.meaning: (of time) to pass, to go by
words.exampleEn: Time really flies.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 가다 (to go) — used for time, not physical movement.

words.meaning: to hold, to lift, to carry
words.exampleEn: I pick up the bag.
words.usageNote: 들다 also means "to cost" (money) — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: This bag costs a lot of money.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 들다 (to hold/lift) — used for money and cost.

words.exampleEn: It takes thirty minutes to get to school.
words.usageNote: 걸리다 also means "to catch" (an illness) — see its own sense card.

words.meaning: to catch (an illness), to get caught
words.exampleEn: I caught a cold.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 걸리다 (to take time) — used for illness or being caught.

words.exampleEn: I lost the game.
words.usageNote: 지다 also describes the sun/moon setting — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: The sun is setting.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 지다 (to lose) — used for the sun or moon.

words.exampleEn: I hang a picture on the wall.
words.usageNote: 걸다 also means "to make a call" (전화를 걸다) — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: I make a phone call to my friend.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 걸다 (to hang) — used with 전화를 for phone calls.

words.exampleEn: Please don't let go.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 놓다 (to put, to place) — used for releasing a grip or letting something go.

words.exampleEn: I stand in line and wait.
words.usageNote: 서다 also means "to stop" (a vehicle or clock) — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: I stand the bottle upright.
words.usageNote: Also means to stop a vehicle.

words.exampleEn: The bus suddenly stopped.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 서다 (to stand) — used for vehicles or machines.

words.exampleEn: I stop the bus.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 세우다 (to stand upright) — used for buses, cars, or clocks.

words.exampleEn: I hit the ball hard.
words.usageNote: 치다 also means "to play" a musical instrument — see its own sense card.

words.meaning: to play (a stringed or percussion instrument)
words.exampleEn: I play the piano.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 치다 (to hit) — used for instruments like 피아노, 기타, 드럼.

words.exampleEn: I untie my shoelaces.
words.usageNote: 풀다 also means "to solve" a problem — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: I solve a math problem.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 풀다 (to untie) — used for problems and questions.

words.exampleEn: The wheel turns quickly.
words.usageNote: 돌다 also means "to go around" a place — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: I went around the park once.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 돌다 (to turn/rotate) — used for moving around a place.

words.exampleEn: I measure the length with a tape measure.
words.usageNote: 재다 also means "to be overly calculating/hesitant" — see its own sense card.

words.meaning: to be overly calculating, to hesitate weighing pros and cons
words.exampleKo: 너무 재지 말고 그냥 해 보세요.
words.exampleEn: Don't overthink it — just try it.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 재다 (to measure) — describes an overly cautious, calculating attitude.
words.exampleVoiceText: 너무 재지 말고 그냥 해 보세요.

words.exampleEn: This soup is too salty.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 짜다 (to weave/put together, a verb) — this is the "salty" adjective sense.

words.meaning: to put together, to organize (a plan)
words.exampleEn: I put together a travel plan.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 짜다 (salty, an adjective) — this is the plan/organize verb sense.

words.exampleEn: I kick the ball hard.
words.usageNote: 차다 also means "to be full" — see its own sense card.

words.meaning: to be full, to fill up
words.exampleEn: The cup is completely full of water.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 차다 (to kick) — used for something filling up.

words.exampleEn: I fell into a puddle.
words.usageNote: 빠지다 also means "to be omitted/left out" — see its own sense card.

words.meaning: to be omitted, to be left out
words.exampleEn: My name was left off the list.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 빠지다 (to fall into) — used for something missing or omitted.

words.exampleEn: A sticker is stuck on the wall.
words.usageNote: 붙다 also means "to pass" (an exam) — see its own sense card.

words.exampleEn: I passed the exam.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 붙다 (to stick) — used for passing a test.

words.exampleKo: 독서는 창의적인 사고 능력을 길러 줍니다.
words.exampleEn: Reading develops creative thinking ability.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 사고 (accident) — used for cognitive thinking or contemplation.
words.exampleVoiceText: 독서는 창의적인 사고 능력을 길러 줍니다.

words.exampleKo: 굴뚝에서 흰 연기가 모락모락 올라가고 있어요.
words.exampleEn: White smoke is rising from the chimney.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 연기 (acting) — refers to the gas and particles emitted by fire.
words.exampleVoiceText: 굴뚝에서 흰 연기가 모락모락 올라가고 있어요.

words.exampleKo: 위인들의 전기를 읽으며 큰 감명을 받았습니다.
words.exampleEn: I was deeply moved by reading the biographies of great people.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 전기 (electricity) — refers to the written account of a person's life.
words.exampleVoiceText: 위인들의 전기를 읽으며 큰 감명을 받았습니다.

words.exampleEn: He was promoted to a director of a large company this year.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 이사 (relocation/moving) — refers to a member of a board of directors.

words.meaning: eating a small amount, light eating, small appetite
words.exampleKo: 건강을 위해서 소식하는 습관을 기르는 것이 좋습니다.
words.exampleEn: It is good to develop a habit of eating small amounts for health.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 소식 (news) — refers to the practice of eating a small amount of food.
words.exampleVoiceText: 건강을 위해서 소식하는 습관을 기르는 것이 좋습니다.

words.exampleEn: A friend is coming.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 와요.
words.formNote: 오다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 와요 because 오 + 아요 contracts to 와요.

words.meaning: to come out, to go out
words.exampleEn: A friend comes out of the house.
words.usageNote: Also means to appear on TV, in the news, or in a program.

words.exampleEn: Water, please.
words.usageNote: Common noun. Often appears in ordering phrases.

words.exampleEn: Did you eat?
words.usageNote: 밥 먹었어요? is also a friendly greeting, like "how are you?".
words.soundNote: 먹었어요 is heard as meogeosseoyo — both the ㄱ and the ㅆ batchim link into the next syllables.

words.exampleEn: The rice is white.
words.usageNote: Cooked rice, the staple food.

words.exampleEn: Korean food is delicious.
words.soundNote: 음식이 is heard as eumsigi (the ㄱ links forward), and 맛있어요 as masisseoyo.

words.exampleEn: I drink coffee.
words.usageNote: A loanword from English.

words.exampleEn: A cup of tea, please.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 차 (car) — this is the tea sense; context decides.

words.exampleEn: I get in the car.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 차 (tea) — this is the car sense; context decides.

words.exampleEn: I like meat.
words.usageNote: 소고기 beef, 돼지고기 pork, 닭고기 chicken.
words.soundNote: 좋아해요 is heard as joahaeyo — the ㅎ of 좋 drops before the vowel.

words.exampleEn: I buy fruit.
I eat bread.
What are you eating?
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 먹어요.
words.formNote: 먹다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 먹어요 by adding the polite present ending -어요.

words.exampleEn: I drink water.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 마셔요.
words.formNote: 마시다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 마셔요 because 시 + 어요 contracts to 셔요.

words.exampleEn: I'm busy today.
See you tomorrow.
What did you do yesterday?
words.soundNote: 했어요 is heard as haesseoyo, not haet-eo-yo — the ㅆ batchim links forward.

words.exampleEn: Do you have time now?
I don't have time.
words.soundNote: 없어요 is heard as eopseoyo — the ㅂ stays put and the ㅅ of the ㅄ batchim links forward.

words.exampleEn: It takes an hour.
words.usageNote: A countable unit of time.

words.exampleEn: I drink coffee in the morning.
words.usageNote: The breakfast sense is separate.

words.exampleEn: I ate breakfast.
words.usageNote: The morning meal.

words.exampleEn: Did you have lunch?
words.usageNote: The noon sense is separate.

words.exampleEn: Let's meet at noon.
words.usageNote: The midday time sense.

words.exampleEn: Let's meet in the evening.
words.usageNote: The dinner sense is separate.

words.exampleEn: I ate dinner.
words.usageNote: The evening meal.

words.exampleEn: It's a nice day.
words.soundNote: 좋은 is heard as joeun (the ㅎ of 좋 drops), and 날이에요 as narieyo (the ㄹ links forward).

words.exampleEn: When are you going?
What are you doing?
words.usageNote: The most useful verb in Korean: 공부하다, 전화하다, 연습하다…
words.formNote: 하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 해요, the normal polite present form of 하다.

words.exampleEn: Do you have time?
words.usageNote: Also means "there is / there are" — see its own sense card. Polite form: 있어요.
words.formNote: 있다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 있어요, the normal polite present form of 있다.

words.exampleEn: There is a book here.
words.usageNote: Existence sense; distinct from 있다 (to have).

words.exampleEn: I don't have time.
words.usageNote: Also means "there is none / nothing is there" — see its own sense card. Polite form: 없어요.
words.formNote: 없다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 없어요, the normal polite present form of 없다.

words.exampleEn: There is nobody in the classroom.
words.usageNote: Absence sense; distinct from 없다 (to not have).

words.exampleEn: I watch a movie.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 봐요.
words.formNote: 보다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 봐요 because 보 + 아요 contracts to 봐요.

words.exampleEn: Please speak slowly.
words.usageNote: 말 (speech) + 하다 (to do).
words.formNote: 말하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 말해 주세요 because 하다-verbs commonly contract to 해요 and 해 주세요 in polite speech.

words.exampleEn: I buy bread.
words.usageNote: Polite present form: 사요.
words.formNote: 사다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 사요, the polite present form of 사다.

words.exampleEn: I'm meeting a friend tomorrow.
words.usageNote: 만나서 반갑습니다 = nice to meet you.
words.formNote: 만나다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 만나요, the polite present form of 만나다.

words.exampleEn: Sleep well.
words.usageNote: 잘 자요 = good night (to someone close).
words.formNote: 자다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 자요, the polite present form of 자다.

words.meaning: to get up, to wake up
words.exampleEn: I get up early in the morning.
words.formNote: 일어나다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 일어나요, the polite present form of 일어나다.

words.exampleEn: I like coffee.
words.usageNote: Takes an object with 을/를, unlike 좋다.
words.formNote: 좋아하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 좋아해요 because 하다 contracts to 해요 in polite speech.

words.exampleEn: The weather is good.
words.usageNote: Describes things: [thing]이/가 좋아요. Compare 좋아하다 (to like).
words.formNote: 좋다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 좋아요, the polite present form of 좋다.
words.soundNote: 좋아요 is heard as joayo because ㅎ drops before the vowel.

words.exampleEn: I don't like rain.
words.usageNote: [thing]이/가 싫어요 = I dislike [thing].
words.formNote: 싫다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 싫어요, the polite present form of 싫다.
words.soundNote: 싫어요 is heard as sireoyo, not silheoyo — the ㅎ of the ㅀ batchim drops and the ㄹ links to the next syllable.

words.exampleEn: The house is big.
words.usageNote: Polite form: 커요. Adjective sense; the verb sense "to grow (up)" is a separate entry.
words.formNote: 크다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 커요 because 크 + 어요 contracts to 커요.

words.exampleEn: My little brother has grown a lot.
words.usageNote: Verb sense: to grow / get bigger (동생이 컸어요). Distinct from the adjective sense "to be big" (집이 커요).
words.formNote: 크다 → 컸어요: as a verb it takes the past ending, 크 + 었어요 → 컸어요.

words.exampleEn: The room is small.
words.usageNote: Polite form: 작아요.
words.formNote: 작다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 작아요, the polite present form of 작다.

words.exampleEn: There are many people.
words.usageNote: Polite form: 많아요.
words.formNote: 많다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 많아요, the polite present form of 많다.

words.exampleEn: There is little time.
words.usageNote: The opposite of 많다.
words.formNote: 적다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 적어요, the polite present form of 적다.

words.exampleEn: This book is fun.
words.usageNote: 재미 (fun) + 있다 (to have). Opposite: 재미없다.
words.formNote: 재미있다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 재미있어요, the polite present form of 재미있다.

words.exampleEn: I'm so tired today.
words.usageNote: Polite form: 피곤해요.
words.formNote: 피곤하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 피곤해요 because 하다 contracts to 해요.

words.exampleEn: This bread is delicious.
words.usageNote: 맛 (taste) + 있다 (to have). Opposite: 맛없다.
words.formNote: 맛있다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 맛있어요, the polite present form of 맛있다.

words.exampleEn: The flowers are pretty.
words.usageNote: Polite form: 예뻐요.
words.formNote: 예쁘다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 예뻐요, the polite present form of 예쁘다.

words.exampleEn: Where are you going?
Why aren't you coming?
How do I get there?
How much is this?
words.usageNote: 얼마예요? is the essential shopping question.

words.exampleEn: What time is it?
words.usageNote: Goes before a counter: 몇 시 (what hour), 몇 명 (how many people).

words.exampleEn: What food do you like?
words.usageNote: Goes before a noun.
words.soundNote: 음식을 is heard as eumsigeul (the ㄱ links forward), and 좋아해요 as joahaeyo (the ㅎ drops).

words.exampleEn: What kind of movie are you watching?
words.usageNote: Asks about qualities or choice among options.

words.exampleEn: How long does it take?
words.usageNote: Asks about degree or duration, not price.

words.exampleEn: I am a student.
words.usageNote: Marks what the sentence is about. Use 는 after a vowel and 은 after a consonant.

words.exampleEn: A friend is coming.
words.usageNote: Marks the subject of the sentence. Use 가 after a vowel and 이 after a consonant.

words.exampleEn: I drink water.
words.usageNote: Marks what the action happens to. Use 를 after a vowel and 을 after a consonant.

words.exampleEn: I'm going home.
words.usageNote: Marks a destination (집에 가요) or a time (아침에).
words.soundNote: 집에 is heard as jibe, not jip-e — a consonant-final noun's last sound links into 에.

words.meaning: at / in (where an action happens); from
words.exampleEn: I study at school.
words.usageNote: Marks where an action happens. 에 marks a destination; 에서 marks activity or a starting point.

words.exampleEn: I'm going too.
words.usageNote: Replaces 은/는 or 이/가 rather than stacking on top of them.

words.exampleEn: It's my friend's book.
words.usageNote: Often pronounced 에 in this role, and frequently dropped in speech.

words.exampleEn: I'm going with a friend.
words.usageNote: Use 와 after a vowel and 과 after a consonant. More formal than 하고.

words.exampleEn: Rice and water, please.
words.usageNote: The everyday spoken "and" between nouns.
words.soundNote: 밥하고 is heard as bapago — the ㅂ and the ㅎ combine into an aspirated p sound.

words.exampleEn: Eat and then go.
words.usageNote: Attaches to a verb stem to chain actions: 먹다 → 먹고.

words.exampleEn: The bag is big.
words.usageNote: A general word for bag, backpack, or purse.

words.exampleEn: I buy shoes.
words.usageNote: Used for shoes in general, even though Korean nouns don't mark plural.

words.exampleEn: The clothes are pretty.
words.usageNote: A general word for clothing.

words.exampleEn: There is a clock on the wall.
words.usageNote: Wall clock sense; distinct from 시계 (watch).

words.exampleEn: I wear a wristwatch.
words.usageNote: Wristwatch sense; distinct from 시계 (clock).

words.exampleEn: I wear glasses.
words.usageNote: 쓰다 (to wear) is used for glasses and hats, not 입다.

words.exampleEn: Do you have an umbrella?
Where is my wallet?
I have a computer.
I watch television.

words.meaning: to appear on TV, in the media
words.exampleEn: The singer appears on TV.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 나오다 (to come out / go out) — used for broadcast or media appearances.

words.exampleEn: The camera is good.
I don't have the key.
I write on paper.
words.usageNote: 에 marks where the writing happens.

words.exampleEn: I have a pen.
I have a pencil.
I need scissors.
words.usageNote: 필요하다 = to need, as in 연습이 필요해요.

words.exampleEn: The battery is dead.
words.usageNote: Literally "there is no battery."

words.exampleEn: Do you have a charger?
I use the internet.
I send an email.
words.usageNote: 보내다 = to send.

words.exampleEn: I take a photo.
words.usageNote: 찍다 = to take (a photo).

words.exampleEn: The room is small.
I sleep in the bed.
I cook in the kitchen.
I clean the room.
words.usageNote: 청소 (cleaning) + 하다 (to do).
words.formNote: 청소하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 청소해요, the polite present form of 청소하다.

words.exampleEn: I wash my hands.
words.formNote: 씻다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 씻어요 by adding -어요; the ㅅ batchim links into the next syllable, so it sounds like ssi-seo-yo.

words.exampleEn: I rest at home.
words.usageNote: Rest sense. The "breathe" sense (숨을 쉬다) is a separate entry.
words.formNote: 쉬다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 쉬어요, the polite present form of 쉬다.

words.exampleEn: I take a deep breath.
words.usageNote: Breathing sense: 숨을 쉬다 = to breathe/take a breath. Distinct from the "to rest" sense (집에서 쉬어요).
words.formNote: 쉬다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 쉬어요, the same polite present form as the "rest" sense.

words.exampleEn: I cook dinner.
words.usageNote: 요리 (cooking) + 하다 (to do).
words.formNote: 요리하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 요리해요, the polite present form of 요리하다.
words.soundNote: 저녁을 is heard as jeonyeogeul — the ㄱ batchim links forward into 을.

words.exampleEn: I shower in the morning.
words.formNote: 샤워하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 샤워해요, the polite present form of 샤워하다.

words.exampleEn: There are many clothes in the closet.
I open the window.
I close the door.
The living room is big.
There is water in the refrigerator.
The dining table is small.
There is a chair.
The desk is big.
I put the book on the desk.
words.usageNote: Also means to let go or release something.

words.exampleEn: I put the book on the desk.
words.usageNote: Used when you place something somewhere and leave it there.

words.exampleEn: I left my umbrella at home.
words.usageNote: Used when you leave something somewhere and go on without it.

words.exampleEn: I open the window.
words.usageNote: Physical open sense. The "hold an event" sense (파티를 열다) is a separate entry.
words.formNote: 열다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 열어요; the ㄹ links into the next syllable, so it sounds like yeo-reo-yo.

words.exampleEn: I threw a party for my friend's birthday.
words.usageNote: Hold-an-event sense: 파티를 열다 = to throw/hold a party, 회의를 열다 = to hold a meeting. Distinct from the physical "open" sense (창문을 열어요).
words.formNote: 열다 → 열었어요: 열 + 었어요 (polite past), the same ㄹ-linking pattern as the "open" sense.

words.exampleEn: I close the door.
words.formNote: 닫다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 닫아요; the ㄷ batchim links into the next syllable, so it sounds like da-da-yo.

words.exampleEn: I turn on the television.
words.formNote: 켜다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 켜요 — stems ending in 여 add 요 directly instead of doubling the ending.

words.exampleEn: I turn off the light.
words.usageNote: 불 = light or fire.
words.formNote: 끄다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 꺼요 because the ㅡ vowel drops and merges before -어요.

words.exampleEn: I go to the airport.
I ride the train.
words.usageNote: 타다 = to ride, to board.

words.exampleEn: I wait for the bus.
words.usageNote: 기다리다 = to wait.

words.exampleEn: The subway is fast.
I call a taxi.
words.usageNote: 부르다 = to call.

words.exampleEn: I sleep at the hotel.
The trip is fun.
words.usageNote: 여행하다 = to travel.

words.exampleEn: I buy a ticket.
I don't know the way.
words.usageNote: Physical road/route sense. Reuses 몰라요 (I don't know) from Survival core. The abstract "way / method" sense is a separate entry.

words.exampleEn: There is no way to solve this problem.
words.usageNote: Abstract sense: a way or means of doing something, often in ~(으)ㄹ 길이 없다 (there's no way to…). Distinct from the physical road sense.

words.exampleEn: I look at the map.
I need a passport.
I have a lot of luggage.
I arrive at the airport.
words.formNote: 도착하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 도착해요, the polite present form of 도착하다.

words.exampleEn: I'm departing now.
words.formNote: 출발하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 출발해요, the polite present form of 출발하다.

words.exampleEn: I book a hotel.
words.formNote: 예약하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 예약해요, the polite present form of 예약하다.

words.exampleEn: The park is big.
I cross the bridge.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 다리 (leg) — this is the bridge sense; context decides.

words.exampleEn: My leg hurts.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 다리 (bridge) — this is the leg sense; context decides.

words.exampleEn: There is water in the bottle.
words.usageNote: Bottle sense; separate counter and illness cards use the same spelling.

words.exampleEn: It's nearby.
The distance is far.
words.usageNote: Distance sense (거리가 멀어요). The "street" sense is a separate entry.

words.exampleEn: There are many people on the street.
words.usageNote: Street sense (거리에 사람이 많아요). Distinct from the distance sense (거리가 멀어요).

words.exampleEn: I don't have money.
What is the price?
words.usageNote: Reuses 얼마예요? from Question words.

words.exampleEn: I pay by card.
words.usageNote: 로 marks the method used, similar to "by" or "with."

words.exampleEn: Do you have cash?
It's on sale.
Receipt, please.
This is cheap.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 싸다 (to pack/wrap, a verb) — this is the "cheap" adjective sense.

words.exampleEn: I pack my bag.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 싸다 (cheap, an adjective) — this is the pack/wrap verb sense.

words.exampleEn: This is expensive.
The price went up.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 오르다 (to climb / go up) — used for prices, numbers, or temperature.

words.exampleEn: I pay by card.
words.formNote: 계산하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 계산해요, the polite present form of 계산하다.

words.exampleEn: Where is the store?
I go to the market.
I buy it at the department store.
The convenience store is close.
There are many customers.
The store clerk is kind.
words.usageNote: 친절하다 = to be kind.

words.exampleEn: They sell bread.
words.formNote: 팔다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 팔아요; the ㄹ links into the next syllable, so it sounds like pa-ra-yo.

words.exampleEn: The size is big.
The color is pretty.
I'll exchange this.
words.formNote: 교환하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 교환해요, the polite present form of 교환하다.

words.exampleEn: Please give me a refund.
words.formNote: 환불하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 환불해 주세요 because 하다-verbs contract to 해 in polite requests.

words.exampleEn: I don't feel well.
words.usageNote: Literally "the body is not good" — a common way to say you feel unwell.

words.exampleEn: I have a headache.
words.usageNote: Body-part sense; distinct from 머리 (hair).

words.exampleEn: I wash my hair.
words.usageNote: Hair on the head; distinct from 머리 (head).

words.exampleEn: I wash my hands.
My foot hurts.
The face is pretty.
I have a stomachache.
words.usageNote: Also means "boat" and "pear" — context decides.

words.exampleEn: My stomach hurts.
words.formNote: 아프다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 아파요 because the ㅡ vowel drops before -아요.

words.exampleEn: I go to the hospital.
I take medicine.
words.usageNote: 먹다 (to eat) is also used for taking medicine.

words.exampleEn: I caught a cold.
words.usageNote: 감기에 걸리다 is the fixed phrase for "to catch a cold."

words.meaning: to get hurt, to get injured
words.exampleEn: I hurt my hand.
words.formNote: 다치다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 다쳐요 because 치 + 어 contracts to 쳐.

words.exampleEn: My throat hurts.
words.usageNote: Throat sense; distinct from 목 (neck).

words.exampleEn: My neck is long.
words.usageNote: Neck sense; distinct from 목 (throat).

words.exampleEn: My shoulder hurts.
My back hurts.
My health is good.
I exercise every day.
words.usageNote: 매일 = every day.
words.formNote: 운동하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 운동해요, the polite present form of 운동하다.

words.exampleEn: I lie down on the bed.
words.formNote: 눕다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 누워요 because ㅂ irregular verbs change ㅂ to 워 before a vowel ending: 눕 + 어요 → 누워요.

words.exampleEn: I have a fever.
Where is the pharmacy?
I am a doctor.
The weather is nice.
It's raining.
words.usageNote: 오다 (to come) is used for rain and snow falling.

words.exampleEn: The wind is blowing.
words.usageNote: 불다 = to blow; a fixed pairing with 바람.

words.exampleEn: His wish is to travel the world.
words.usageNote: Used for a hope or wish, not the weather noun.

words.exampleEn: It's hot today.
words.formNote: 덥다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 더워요 because ㅂ irregular verbs change ㅂ to 워 before a vowel ending: 덥 + 어요 → 더워요.

words.exampleEn: It's cold today.
words.formNote: 춥다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 추워요 because ㅂ irregular verbs change ㅂ to 워 before a vowel ending: 춥 + 어요 → 추워요.

words.exampleEn: The wind is strong.
words.usageNote: Used for wind, waves, or force being strong.

words.exampleEn: The weather is warm.
words.formNote: 따뜻하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 따뜻해요, the polite present form of 따뜻하다.
words.soundNote: 따뜻해요 is heard as ttatteutaeyo — the ㅅ batchim combines with the following ㅎ into an aspirated t sound.

words.exampleEn: The breeze is cool.
words.formNote: 시원하다 is the dictionary form. In this sentence it becomes 시원해요, the polite present form of 시원하다.

words.exampleEn: The sky is pretty.
The tree is big.
The flowers are pretty.
I like this season.
I like spring.
Summer is hot.
Autumn is pretty.
Winter is cold.
It's snowing.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 눈 (eye) — this is the snow sense. 오다 (to come) is used for snow falling, like rain.

words.exampleEn: The eyes are big.
words.usageNote: Homophone of 눈 (snow) — this is the eye sense; context decides.

words.exampleEn: The sun is bright.
The moon is pretty.
There are many stars.
The sea is big.
Where are you going?
words.usageNote: Casual 반말 ending for close friends or someone younger. Add 요 to make it polite: 가 → 가요.

words.exampleEn: I'm going home now.
words.usageNote: The everyday polite ending. Vowel harmony: 아요 after ㅏ/ㅗ stems, otherwise 어요.

words.exampleEn: I am going now.
words.usageNote: Formal ending for announcements, presentations, and the workplace. ㅂ니다 after a vowel stem (가다 → 갑니다), 습니다 after a consonant stem.

words.exampleEn: Oh, the weather is nice!
words.usageNote: Polite ending that shows you just noticed or realized something.

words.exampleEn: Shall we go together?
words.usageNote: Polite way to suggest doing something together or to wonder aloud. 을까요 after a consonant stem, ㄹ까요 after a vowel stem.

words.exampleEn: I'm not going.
words.usageNote: Goes right before the verb or adjective for simple negation. With 하다 verbs it splits the noun: 공부 안 해요.

words.exampleEn: I can't go today.
words.usageNote: Marks inability or impossibility, placed before the verb. With 하다 verbs: 운동 못 해요.

words.exampleEn: I don't eat spicy things.
words.usageNote: Attach 지 않다 to the stem and conjugate 않다. Same meaning as 안, but more explicit or formal.

words.exampleEn: I was so busy I couldn't sleep.
words.usageNote: Long form of 못. Attach to the stem and conjugate 못하다.

words.exampleEn: I met a friend yesterday.
words.usageNote: The polite past ending: past marker 았/었 plus 어요. 았 after ㅏ/ㅗ stems, otherwise 었.

words.exampleEn: If I have time, let's meet.
words.usageNote: Sets a condition: if or when the first clause happens, the second follows. 으면 after a consonant stem, 면 after a vowel stem.

words.exampleEn: I came to eat.
words.usageNote: Shows the purpose of going or coming. Used with movement verbs like 가다 and 오다.

words.exampleEn: On weekends I sleep or rest.
words.usageNote: Links choices between verbs or clauses: do this or that.

words.exampleEn: As soon as I got home, I slept.
words.usageNote: The second action happens right after the first.

words.exampleEn: On the way home, I ran into a friend.
words.usageNote: One action is interrupted or switches to another mid-way.

words.exampleEn: I didn't go because of the rain.
words.usageNote: Attaches to a noun to give a reason. After a verb, use 기 때문에.

words.exampleEn: It's the person who is eating.
words.usageNote: Turns a verb into a modifier before a noun, showing present or ongoing action.

words.exampleEn: It's the rice I ate.
words.usageNote: Marks a finished action modifying the noun. It looks identical to the adjective modifier, so context decides.

words.exampleEn: It's the rice I'll eat tomorrow.
words.usageNote: Shows an action that has not happened yet: future or intended.

words.exampleEn: It's a good person.
words.usageNote: Descriptive predicates take (으)ㄴ to modify a noun (좋다 → 좋은). Verbs use 는 for the present.

words.exampleEn: It's the one I bought.
words.usageNote: A dependent noun meaning thing or one. Combine it with a modifier form to turn a clause into a noun. Often shortened to 거.

words.exampleEn: The teacher is coming now.
words.usageNote: Raises respect toward the sentence's subject. It fuses into endings: 가시 + 어요 → 가세요. This is separate from politeness toward the listener (요/습니다).

words.meaning: to be / stay (honorific of 있다, for people)
words.exampleEn: Grandmother is at home.
words.usageNote: Honorific replacement for 있다 when the subject is a respected person. Polite form: 계세요.

words.exampleEn: Father is eating a meal.
words.usageNote: Polite honorific for eating or drinking. Polite form: 드세요. 잡수시다 is even more formal.

words.exampleEn: Grandfather is sleeping.
words.usageNote: Honorific replacement for 자다. Polite form: 주무세요.

words.exampleEn: May I ask your name?
words.usageNote: Honorific noun for someone's name, used when asking politely.

words.exampleEn: May I ask your age?
words.usageNote: Honorific noun for age, used for elders.

words.exampleEn: I walk in the park.
words.usageNote: ㄷ irregular: the final ㄷ becomes ㄹ before a vowel ending, so 걷다 → 걸어요.
words.formNote: 걷다 is the dictionary form. As a ㄷ irregular verb the ㄷ changes to ㄹ before a vowel ending: 걷 + 어요 → 걸어요.

words.exampleEn: Kimchi is spicy.
words.usageNote: ㅂ irregular: the final ㅂ changes to 우 before a vowel, so 맵다 → 매워요.
words.formNote: 맵다 is the dictionary form. As a ㅂ irregular the ㅂ changes to 워 before a vowel ending: 맵 + 어요 → 매워요.

words.exampleEn: I build a house.
words.usageNote: Build-a-structure sense. ㅅ irregular: the final ㅅ drops before a vowel, with no contraction, so 짓다 → 지어요. The "make/prepare" sense (밥을 짓다, 이름을 짓다) is a separate entry.
words.formNote: 짓다 is the dictionary form. As a ㅅ irregular the ㅅ drops before a vowel ending, but the vowels do not contract: 짓 + 어요 → 지어요.

words.exampleEn: Mom makes rice.
words.usageNote: Make/prepare sense: 밥을 짓다 = to cook rice, 이름을 짓다 = to give a name. Same ㅅ irregular as the "build" sense: 짓 + 어요 → 지어요, no contraction.
words.formNote: 짓다 is the dictionary form. As a ㅅ irregular the ㅅ drops before a vowel ending, but the vowels do not contract: 짓 + 어요 → 지어요.

words.exampleEn: The apple is red.
words.usageNote: ㅎ irregular: the final ㅎ drops and the vowel shifts, so 빨갛다 → 빨개요. Common in color adjectives.
words.formNote: 빨갛다 is the dictionary form. As a ㅎ irregular the ㅎ drops and the ending vowel merges: 빨갛 + 아요 → 빨개요.

words.exampleEn: The train is fast.
words.usageNote: 르 irregular: 르 becomes ㄹㄹ before 아/어, so 빠르다 → 빨라요.
words.formNote: 빠르다 is the dictionary form. As a 르 irregular the 르 doubles the ㄹ before 아/어: 빠르 + 아요 → 빨라요.

words.exampleEn: I live in Seoul.
words.usageNote: Residence sense. ㄹ-deletion: the stem ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ (삽니다, 사세요, 사는), though it stays in 살아요. The "be alive / survive" sense is a separate entry.
words.formNote: 살다 keeps its ㄹ in 살아요, but the ㄹ drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ endings: 살 + ㅂ니다 → 삽니다.

words.exampleEn: Fortunately, the driver survived the accident.
words.usageNote: Be-alive/survive sense, distinct from residence. Same ㄹ-deletion pattern as the residence sense.
words.formNote: 살다 keeps its ㄹ before a vowel ending: 살 + 았어요 → 살았어요.

words.exampleEn: Try eating Korean food.
words.usageNote: Auxiliary verb used after -아/어 to mean 'try doing something'.
words.formNote: 보다 here functions as an auxiliary verb. In the example, 먹다 conjugates to 먹어, followed by 봐요.

words.exampleEn: What did you say?
words.usageNote: Used to quote speech or ask what someone said (contraction of -고 하다).
words.formNote: 하다 conjugates to 했어요 in the past tense to mean 'said'.

words.meaning: to occur, to happen, to arise
words.exampleEn: An accident happened on the street.
words.usageNote: Used when events, thoughts, or feelings happen or break out.
words.formNote: 나다 conjugates to 났어요 in the past tense.

words.meaning: to grow, to sprout, to come out

words.usageNote: Used for teeth/hair growing, plants sprouting, or sweat/tears coming out.
words.formNote: 나다 is regular. It conjugates to 나요 in the polite present form.

words.meaning: abandonment / giving up / bunch / counter for cabbage
words.meaningShort: abandonment / giving up / bunch / counter for cabbage
words.exampleKo: 어려운 상황 앞에서도 꿈을 절대 포기하지 마세요.
words.exampleEn: Never give up on your dreams even in front of difficult situations.
words.exampleVoiceText: 어려운 상황 앞에서도 꿈을 절대 포기하지 마세요.

words.exampleKo: 은행 모바일 앱으로 안전한 송금 거래를 끝마쳤어요.
words.exampleEn: I finished the safe remittance transaction with the bank mobile app.
words.exampleVoiceText: 은행 모바일 앱으로 안전한 송금 거래를 끝마쳤어요.

words.exampleKo: 어깨 통증으로 고통을 겪고 있어서 침을 맞았어요.
words.exampleEn: I got acupuncture because I am suffering from shoulder pain.
words.exampleVoiceText: 어깨 통증으로 고통을 겪고 있어서 침을 맞았어요.

words.exampleKo: 국회에서 오늘 오후 새로운 예산안 정책이 통과되었어요.
words.exampleEn: A new budget policy passed in the National Assembly this afternoon.
words.exampleVoiceText: 국회에서 오늘 오후 새로운 예산안 정책이 통과되었어요.

words.exampleKo: 박물관 전시실 내부에는 고대 전쟁 무기들이 가득해요.
words.exampleEn: The museum exhibition room interior is filled with ancient war weapons.
words.exampleVoiceText: 박물관 전시실 내부에는 고대 전쟁 무기들이 가득해요.

words.exampleKo: 친구에게 약속 장소 위치를 알리는 문자를 보냈어요.
words.exampleEn: I sent a text message notifying my friend of the appointment place location.
words.exampleVoiceText: 친구에게 약속 장소 위치를 알리는 문자를 보냈어요.

words.exampleKo: 꽃밭에서 나비를 쫓아 뛰어노는 소녀의 모습이 예뻐요.
words.exampleEn: The image of the girl running and playing chasing butterflies in the flower garden is pretty.
words.exampleVoiceText: 꽃밭에서 나비를 쫓아 뛰어노는 소녀의 모습이 예뻐요.

words.meaning: always / all the time / at all times
words.meaningShort: always / all the time / at all times
words.exampleKo: 그는 약속 시간보다 언제나 일찍 도착하는 편이에요.
words.exampleEn: He tends to always arrive earlier than the appointment time.
words.exampleVoiceText: 그는 약속 시간보다 언제나 일찍 도착하는 편이에요.

words.exampleKo: 영화 결말의 슬픈 장면을 보며 눈물을 흘렸어요.
words.exampleEn: I shed tears looking at the sad scene of the movie ending.
words.exampleVoiceText: 영화 결말의 슬픈 장면을 보며 눈물을 흘렸어요.

words.exampleKo: 수학 교과서 첫 장에 나오는 공식의 정의를 읽었어요.
words.exampleEn: I read the definition of the formula in the first chapter of the math textbook.
words.exampleVoiceText: 수학 교과서 첫 장에 나오는 공식의 정의를 읽었어요.

words.exampleKo: 그가 회의 시간에 낸 아이디어 제안이 채택되었습니다.
words.exampleEn: The idea suggestion he made during the meeting time was adopted.
words.exampleVoiceText: 그가 회의 시간에 낸 아이디어 제안이 채택되었습니다.

words.exampleKo: 상대방의 이야기를 진심 어린 태도로 경청해야 해요.
words.exampleEn: You must listen carefully to the other party's story with a sincere attitude.
words.exampleVoiceText: 상대방의 이야기를 진심 어린 태도로 경청해야 해요.

words.exampleKo: 시끄러운 소음 속에서도 공부방 집중력을 잃지 마세요.
words.exampleEn: Do not lose study room concentration even in noisy noise.
words.exampleVoiceText: 시끄러운 소음 속에서도 공부방 집중력을 잃지 마세요.

words.exampleKo: 두 식물 종류의 형태적 특징 차이를 분석해 보았습니다.
words.exampleEn: I analyzed the morphological characteristic differences of the two plant kinds.
words.exampleVoiceText: 두 식물 종류의 형태적 특징 차이를 분석해 보았습니다.

words.exampleKo: 정부 기관의 신속한 행정 처리 덕분에 편해졌어요.
words.exampleEn: Thanks to the quick administrative processing of government agencies, it became convenient.
words.exampleVoiceText: 정부 기관의 신속한 행정 처리 덕분에 편해졌어요.

words.exampleEn: I cut off the internet.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 끊다 (to quit). Used for lines, electricity, internet, or other connections.

words.exampleEn: I quit coffee.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 끊다 (to cut off) — used for giving up a habit like coffee or smoking.

words.exampleEn: I unplugged the phone charger.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 빼다 (to subtract) — used for taking something out of a bag, box, socket, or list.

words.exampleEn: I subtract 3 from 10.
words.usageNote: Distinct sense from 빼다 (to take out/remove) — used with numbers or money.

words.meaning: to remain, to be left over
words.exampleEn: I have money left over.
words.usageNote: One beginner row covers what remains after use, including leftover food, extra time, or money.

words.exampleEn: I close my eyes.
words.usageNote: With 눈, this means to close your eyes. Distinct from 감다 (to wash hair).

words.exampleEn: I wash my hair.
words.usageNote: With 머리, this means to wash your hair. Distinct from 감다 (to close your eyes).

words.exampleEn: This cake is sweet.
words.usageNote: Not the verb sense 달다 (to hang or attach).

words.exampleEn: I hang a picture on the wall.
words.usageNote: Not the adjective sense 달다 (sweet).
